data.diagnosis: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
data.description: A rare low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor, usually occurring in young women but occasionally seen in older men. It is typically a large, well-circumscribed, heterogeneous solid and cystic mass with hemorrhagic or necrotic areas. Histology commonly shows uniform tumor cells with solid and pseudopapillary growth patterns.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion due to mass effect or pancreatic involvement
Minimal or absent abdominal pain despite a large pancreatic mass
Large heterogeneous pancreatic-region mass on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 73 years, since this tumor is much more common in young women
Male sex
Diabetes and elevated fasting glucose are not characteristic presenting features

data.description: A rare malignant pancreatic exocrine tumor composed of cells showing acinar differentiation. Some tumors have yellow-tan cut surfaces due to necrosis or lipid-rich change.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of jaundice or major laboratory abnormalities can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain

data.description: A neoplasm arising from pancreatic neuroendocrine cells. Nonfunctioning tumors may grow silently until they become large and produce abdominal distention, early satiety, digestive symptoms, or a palpable abdominal mass. Imaging may show a hypervascular solid pancreatic lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Diabetes may occur with pancreatic endocrine dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: No symptoms of hormone excess, such as hypoglycemia, diarrhea, flushing, peptic ulcer disease, or recurrent rash

Pseudopapillary histologic features would not be typical

A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

data.description: An autosomal-dominant acantholytic disorder caused by ATP2C1 mutations, characterized by recurrent painful, pruritic erosions, fissures, crusting, and occasional vesicles or blisters in flexural areas. Heat, sweating, friction, and secondary infection commonly worsen disease.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic recurrent rash in the axillae
Family history of a similar axillary rash in his sister
Maceration, erosion, crusting, and malodor in an intertriginous area
Normal nails and oral mucosa, which is compatible with Hailey-Hailey disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation are not core features, although postinflammatory pigment change can occur
Multiple acrochordons are not a typical primary manifestation
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is unrelated to the disease

data.description: An inherited acantholytic keratinization disorder caused by ATP2A2 mutations. It typically produces greasy crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic regions and skin folds, often exacerbated by heat, sweating, and ultraviolet exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic inherited-appearing skin disorder with an affected sibling
Occasional erosions and blistering in flexural skin
Acantholytic changes can be seen histologically
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions are confined predominantly to the axillae rather than widespread seborrheic sites
No characteristic nail abnormalities such as V-shaped nicking or red-and-white longitudinal streaks
No oral mucosal papules
No classic widespread greasy keratotic papules
No significant sun exposure, whereas ultraviolet light often exacerbates Darier disease

data.diagnosis: Acanthosis nigricans associated with obesity and insulin resistance
data.description: A velvety, thickened, hyperpigmented plaque disorder most commonly affecting axillae, neck, and groin. It is frequently associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and diabetes mellitus.
symptoms_not_in_common: Painful and pruritic rash
Recurrent summer flares
Blisters
Maceration, erosions, and malodorous crusting
Acantholysis on histology
Family history of a similar recurrent erosive axillary rash

data.diagnosis: Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or candidal infection
data.description: Inflammation of opposing skin surfaces caused by moisture, friction, heat, and sweating. It may become secondarily infected with Candida or bacteria, producing maceration, erosions, malodor, crusting, and discomfort.
symptoms_in_common: Overweight status, which increases friction and moisture retention
symptoms_not_in_common: Five-year familial history of a similar rash in a sibling
Intermittent blistering as a major feature
Acantholytic histologic findings
Persistent irregular pigmentary changes and numerous lesions suggestive of an inherited dermatosis

Her symptoms continued to progress and she became wheelchair-bound 6 months later. When reviewed at institution, she was severely disabled requiring regular IVIG treatments at a dose of 90g every 12 days. She was taking regular diazepam at a dose of 30mg per day and morphine up to 60mg a day to control pain. On examination, she had brisk reflexes and severe clonus. The muscle spasms were severe enough to compromise her breathing and she required intermittent oxygen.

http_response.description:
60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and adalimumab, admitted after a burn from an electric heater. Four months earlier she developed pain and stiffness in the MCP and IP joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the ankles. Labs then showed anemia, leukopenia/neutropenia, rheumatoid factor elevation, hypergammaglobulinemia, ANA 1:640, low C4, mildly positive anti-dsDNA, and positive cryoglobulins; HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests were negative. On admission she had fever and pancytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy; blood film, cultures, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, CMV PCR, and tuberculin test were negative. She had traveled to Athens seven months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

data.description: A chronic granulomatous skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, typically causing slowly enlarging yellow-brown or reddish plaques with central atrophy, induration, and telangiectasia on the shins. symptoms_not_in_common: Young age of 25 years, as necrobiosis lipoidica is more often diagnosed in middle-aged adults

14-year-old boy with 2 days of acute fear of choking and difficulty swallowing սկսed after choking on chicken at dinner, followed by vomiting with attempted eating, markedly reduced oral intake, and drooling; on the day of presentation he took only small sips of water and slept most of the day. Mother reported inspiratory stridor during sleep over the preceding few weeks. Past history includes infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, sensory-integration training in childhood, keratosis pilaris, and eczema; immunizations were incomplete after age 2.5 years. Examination showed an alert, anxious-appearing boy with persistent involuntary burping, dry oral mucosa, and drooling; vital signs were stable. 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with recurrent fever. Four months earlier, she developed bleeding from a right scalp lesion; biopsy showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months before admission, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which showed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 lymph nodes; BRAF V600E mutation was identified. One month before admission, she started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib, and developed fever and nausea within 1 day; symptoms resolved after stopping treatment and giving antipyretics. Fever recurred 2 weeks before admission. On presentation, she had a temperature of 40.2°C, pulse 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 85/53 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, appeared ill and diaphoretic, had mild right upper quadrant tenderness, and no rash.

Hip pain with restricted or painful movement

Possible association with autoimmune serologies such as positive antinuclear antibody

No reported facial disfigurement, ectropion, or mucosal involvement

symptoms_in_common: Hyperkeratotic, ulcerated, crusted, and keratin-filled nodules
History of kidney transplantation with prior immunosuppression, a major squamous cell carcinoma risk factor

data.diagnosis: Acquired perforating dermatosis associated with chronic renal failure

15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst who initially presented with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later, she developed acute lower back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission, she had mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, no fever or meningism, and a GCS of 15. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia. By day 2, she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffman signs. CSF and electromyography were normal; PCR detected high Zika virus levels in serum, urine, and CSF, with other infectious and autoimmune studies negative.

Upper motor neuron signs including bilateral Hoffman signs

data.diagnosis: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), mature cortical-type immunophenotype
data.description: An aggressive hematologic malignancy of T-lymphoid precursor cells, typically presenting with circulating blasts, bone-marrow involvement, thrombocytopenia, and high LDH. The CD2+, CD3+, CD5+, and CD7+ phenotype supports T-lineage leukemia; the reported X;14 and 12;14 rearrangements involving the T-cell receptor alpha/delta locus are compatible with a T-ALL-associated genetic abnormality.
symptoms_in_common: Headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting, which may reflect leukostasis or central nervous system involvement
Blasts positive for T-cell markers CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
Absence of B-cell markers CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22

symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable lymph-node enlargement
No hepatosplenomegaly
